original_question: Does every convex 3-polytope admit a nonoverlapping net, that is, can one cut the polytope along some collection of edges so that the resulting connected surface unfolds into the plane without self-overlap?
target_in_paper: Section 9, "Dürer’s Conjecture" (the paper’s unlabeled restatement of Dürer’s unfolding problem).
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the same mathematical question as the paper: it is about every 3-dimensional polytope, it restricts cuts to edges, it requires the cut surface to remain connected, and it asks for a planar unfolding with no overlap. That matches the paper’s definition of a net and its summary of Dürer’s conjecture.
missing_details: The paper’s official terminology is "net (or unfolding)" of a 3-polytope; naming that explicitly makes the question more paper-faithful.

The paper states the conjecture as "any polytope has a nonoverlapping net" immediately after defining nets only for 3-polytopes, so the 3-dimensional scope should be made explicit in the stand-alone version.
To align exactly with Section 9, it should be explicit that the allowed cuts are only along edges and that the cut surface is a single connected shape before being flattened into the plane.

There are no additional algebraic conditions here: no ambient ring or field, no degree or homogeneity assumptions, no nilpotency condition, and no asymptotic quantifier such as "for all sufficiently large m". The only hidden assumptions are geometric ones about dimension, edge cuts, connectedness, and nonoverlap of the planar development.
refined_question: Does every 3-dimensional convex polytope admit a nonoverlapping net (or unfolding); that is, can one cut the polytope along some of its edges so that the resulting connected surface can be flattened into the plane without overlap?
justification: In this paper, the relevant target is the unlabeled open problem in Section 9 rather than any numbered conjecture from another article. Section 9 first defines a net (or unfolding) of a 3-polytope as what results from cutting along edges so that the connected shape can be flattened into the plane, and then states Dürer’s conjecture as the claim that any polytope has a nonoverlapping net. The refined question keeps exactly that scope and language, while making explicit the 3-dimensional setting and the edge-cut and connectedness requirements needed for the question to stand alone. Section 1 also confirms that the paper specifically revisits Dürer’s conjecture in Section 9.
